question.text: Per NISM Section 1.4.4.1, which statement BEST captures the interdependence between the primary and secondary markets as relevant to a Cat III AIF raising capital and deploying it?

answer.text: Primary and secondary markets operate independently; activity in one has no bearing on the other.

The primary market facilitates CREATION of financial assets, while the secondary market facilitates their MARKETABILITY/TRADABILITY. They are interdependent and inseparable — an active secondary market promotes the primary market because investors are assured of an exit.
Only the secondary market falls under SEBI jurisdiction; the primary market is regulated by RBI.
Primary market trades happen between investors; secondary market trades happen between issuer and investor.

explanation.text: The Logic: Section 1.4.4.1 states: 'The primary market facilitates creation of financial assets, and the secondary market facilitates their marketability/tradability which makes these two segments of Financial Markets - interdependent and inseparable. Thus, in the primary market, the issuers have direct contact with the investors, while in the secondary market, the dealings are between investors only.' An active secondary market directly supports primary issuance by assuring exit. The Trap: Option A contradicts the interdependence thesis. Option C is factually wrong — both fall under SEBI. Option D inverts the definitions (primary is issuer-to-investor; secondary is investor-to-investor). Cross-Exam Context: XXI-B (PM), X-A (IA L1), and III-A (Compliance) all test primary-vs-secondary distinctions. XIX-E frames it for Cat III — a healthy secondary market in listed equity is WHY Cat III long-short works: daily NAV strikes, rapid position unwind, and prime-broker stock-borrow all depend on deep secondary-market liquidity. Manager's Pro-Tip: Cat III strategies depend critically on secondary-market depth — a sudden drop in ADVs (like in March 2020) can force wider bid-ask spreads and slippage on stop-loss exits. Build a liquidity-adjusted position-limit framework: cap each holding at X% of 30-day ADV (typically 10-15% for liquid large-caps, 5% for mid-caps) so the fund can exit within T+2 without moving the market — this keeps the fund's NAV honest and protects redeeming investors.
